name: Learn: Canary Deployments
objective: CKAD › Application Deployment. Run a new version alongside the stable one behind ONE Service and split traffic by replica ratio (label-based canary), then diagnose a canary that gets no traffic. Graded exactly.
description: Build a label-based canary: stable + canary Deployments sharing an app label, one Service fronting both, verify the split, and fix a canary that's excluded by a too-specific selector.

questions.title: Deploy the stable version
questions.teach:
A **canary** release runs the new version beside the stable one and gives it a slice of traffic. Both Deployments share a label (`app=web`) that one Service selects, so traffic splits by **replica ratio**. Start with stable.

**Gotcha:** each Deployment's own `selector` must include a distinguishing label (`track`) so it manages only *its* pods, not the other's.
questions.prompt:
In `canary-learn`, create Deployment `web-stable`: image `nginx:1.25`, **3** replicas, pod labels `app=web` AND `track=stable`, with its selector matching **both** labels.

Target: `web-stable` — nginx:1.25, 3 replicas, pod labels + selector `app=web`/`track=stable`.
questions.hint: Selector `matchLabels: {app: web, track: stable}`; pod template labels the same. 3 replicas.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web-stable, namespace: canary-learn }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web, track: stable } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web, track: stable } }
    spec:
      containers: [ { name: web, image: nginx:1.25 } ]
YAML
questions.eli5:
Imagine your website is a snack shop, and right now it's serving everyone from one trusted recipe. Before you let a brand-new recipe loose on all your customers, you want to keep the old, reliable one running first. This step is you setting up that trusted old shop.

A **Deployment** is like a manager you hire and tell: *"Always keep exactly 3 identical snack stands open, all using recipe nginx:1.25."* If a stand breaks, the manager opens a new one. You put name tags on each stand so you (and later a waiter) can find them.

The name tags here are **labels**:
- `app=web` — "this is part of the website" (the shared tag).
- `track=stable` — "this is the old, trusted recipe."

The manager also has a **selector** — a note saying *"the stands I'm responsible for wear BOTH these tags."* The selector and the tags on the stands must match, or the manager gets confused about which stands are his.

**Watch out for:**

- **The selector must match the pod's labels exactly.** If the stands wear `app=web, track=stable` but the manager only looks for `app=web`, the Deployment is rejected or grabs the wrong stands.
- **Include the distinguishing `track` label in the selector**, so this manager only counts *his* stable stands and not the canary ones you add next.
- **The selector is immutable** — once the Deployment is created you cannot change it. Fix mistakes by deleting and recreating.
- **Replicas = 3** exactly. Too few or too many and the traffic math later will be wrong.
questions.deepDive:
## Deploy the stable version — full rundown

### Mental model
A **canary release** runs the new version *beside* the stable one and gives it a slice of real traffic. In the label-based approach there's no service mesh — the split is pure **replica arithmetic** behind one Service. This first step stands up the **stable** Deployment that will carry the majority of traffic.

Three label roles are in play:
- `app=web` — the **shared** label a single Service will select on (added in step 3).
- `track=stable` / `track=canary` — the **distinguishing** label that keeps each Deployment managing only its own pods.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-stable
  namespace: canary-learn
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
      track: stable        # selector matches BOTH labels
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
        track: stable       # pod labels must be a superset of selector
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25
```

Apply and verify:
```bash
kubectl apply -f web-stable.yaml
kubectl -n canary-learn get deploy web-stable
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l app=web -L track
```

### Field reference
| Field | Meaning | Here |
|---|---|---|
| `spec.replicas` | desired pod count | `3` |
| `spec.selector.matchLabels` | which pods this Deployment owns (immutable) | `app=web, track=stable` |
| `spec.template.metadata.labels` | labels stamped on each pod | `app=web, track=stable` |
| `spec.template.spec.containers[].image` | container image | `nginx:1.25` |

### The selector/label contract
The Deployment's `selector.matchLabels` **must be a subset** of `template.metadata.labels`. If the template labels don't cover the selector, the API server rejects the Deployment:

```
selector does not match template labels
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Selector is immutable.** You cannot `kubectl edit` or `apply` a changed `spec.selector` on an existing Deployment — you must delete and recreate. Get it right the first time.
- **Must include `track` in the selector**, not just `app=web`. If both Deployments selected only `app=web`, each would try to own the *other's* pods and the replica counts would fight.
- **Replica count is graded exactly** — `3`, not 2 or 4; the traffic ratio in later steps depends on it.
- A bare `kubectl create deployment` only sets one label (`app=<name>`) and no `track` — hand-write YAML or patch labels when you need two.
- Namespace matters: everything lives in `canary-learn`; forgetting `-n`/`namespace:` puts it in `default`.

### Quick reference
```bash
# imperative skeleton, then edit to add labels/selector:
kubectl -n canary-learn create deployment web-stable \
  --image=nginx:1.25 --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > web-stable.yaml
# edit: add track=stable to selector.matchLabels AND template.metadata.labels
kubectl apply -f web-stable.yaml

kubectl -n canary-learn get deploy web-stable -o wide
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l track=stable
```

questions.title: Deploy the canary version
questions.teach:
Add the canary Deployment: new image, the **same** `app=web` label (so the Service picks it up) plus `track=canary`. With 3 stable : 1 canary replicas, the canary gets ~25% of traffic.

**Gotcha:** the shared `app=web` label is what puts canary pods behind the Service; `track` keeps the two Deployments separate.
questions.prompt:
In `canary-learn`, create Deployment `web-canary`: image `nginx:1.26`, **1** replica, pod labels `app=web` AND `track=canary`, selector matching both.

Target: `web-canary` — nginx:1.26, 1 replica, pod labels + selector `app=web`/`track=canary`.
questions.hint: Same shape as web-stable but `track: canary`, image `nginx:1.26`, 1 replica.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web-canary, namespace: canary-learn }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web, track: canary } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web, track: canary } }
    spec:
      containers: [ { name: web, image: nginx:1.26 } ]
YAML
questions.eli5:
Now you've got a new snack recipe (nginx:1.26) and you want a *few* customers to try it before you bet the whole shop on it. So you open **one** new stand running the new recipe, right next to the three trusted ones.

This new stand is the **canary** — like the little bird miners used to carry to warn them of trouble. If the new recipe is bad, only a small number of customers notice, and you shut it down fast.

You hire a second manager (a second Deployment, `web-canary`) and tell them: *"Keep exactly 1 stand open, running nginx:1.26."* The crucial trick is the name tags:
- `app=web` — the **same** shared tag as the stable stands. This is what lets the future waiter (the Service) hand customers to this stand too.
- `track=canary` — marks it as the experimental one, so the two managers don't step on each other.

With 3 old stands and 1 new stand, roughly 1 in 4 customers (about 25%) will land on the new recipe — just by counting stands.

**Watch out for:**

- **The `app=web` label must be identical** to the stable pods' — same key, same value. A typo like `app=Web` and the Service silently ignores this stand, so the canary gets 0 customers.
- **`track=canary` must differ from stable**, or the two managers will both try to own the same stands.
- **The selector must match both labels** and, like before, it's **immutable** — recreate to fix.
- **1 replica**, exactly — the whole point is a *small* slice. More replicas means a bigger, riskier exposure.
questions.deepDive:
## Deploy the canary version — full rundown

### Mental model
The canary is a **small second Deployment** running the new image, deliberately given few replicas. It shares the `app=web` label with stable so a single Service fronts both; the `track=canary` label keeps it a separate, independently scalable unit. Traffic share = canary endpoints ÷ total endpoints.

With **3 stable : 1 canary**, the canary receives roughly **1/4 ≈ 25%** of requests.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-canary
  namespace: canary-learn
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
      track: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
        track: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.26
```

### Replica ratio → traffic ratio
| stable replicas | canary replicas | total endpoints | canary share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 4 | ~25% |
| 9 | 1 | 10 | ~10% |
| 1 | 1 | 2 | ~50% |
| 1 | 3 | 4 | ~75% |

kube-proxy load-balances across ready endpoints roughly evenly, so the ratio is approximate, not guaranteed per-request.

### Promote / roll back (the lifecycle this enables)
```bash
# shift more traffic to canary
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-canary --replicas=3

# PROMOTE: canary becomes the fleet, retire stable
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-canary --replicas=4
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-stable --replicas=0

# ROLL BACK: just remove the canary
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-canary --replicas=0
# or: kubectl -n canary-learn delete deploy web-canary
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Same `app` label, exact match.** The shared label is the *only* thing tying the canary to the Service. `app=web` vs `app=Web` vs `app=webapp` → canary silently excluded, 0% traffic.
- **Different `track` value** is mandatory — two Deployments must not share an identical selector or they fight over the same pods.
- **Selector immutable** — recreate to fix a bad selector.
- **1 replica exactly** — graded; the point of a canary is a *small* blast radius.
- This is **replica-ratio** canary, not percentage-exact. For precise percentages you'd need an ingress controller or service mesh (out of scope here).
- A canary pod that never becomes **Ready** contributes **no endpoint** → still gets 0% (see step 4).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n canary-learn create deployment web-canary \
  --image=nginx:1.26 --replicas=1 --dry-run=client -o yaml > web-canary.yaml
# edit selector.matchLabels AND template labels to { app: web, track: canary }
kubectl apply -f web-canary.yaml
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l app=web -L track   # 3 stable + 1 canary
```

questions.title: One Service fronting both
questions.teach:
One **Service** fronts both Deployments by selecting only the **shared** label (`app=web`) — NOT `track`. It load-balances across every matching ready pod, so the replica ratio becomes the traffic ratio.

**Gotcha:** if the Service selector includes `track`, it fronts only one version and the other gets no traffic.
questions.prompt:
Create a ClusterIP Service `web` in `canary-learn` (port 80 → targetPort 80) selecting **only** `app=web` (no `track`), so it fronts both stable and canary.

Target: Service `web` ClusterIP, port 80→80, selector is exactly `app=web`.
questions.hint: `spec.selector: {app: web}` — just the shared label, no track.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web, namespace: canary-learn }
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
YAML

verification.description: Service web: ClusterIP 80->80, selector exactly app=web

questions.eli5:
You now have four snack stands open — three old, one new — but customers don't know where to go. You need **one front counter** that takes every customer and sends them to whichever stand is free. That front counter is a **Service**.

A Service is a waiter with a clipboard. On the clipboard is a **selector**: a rule for *which stands count as "the website."* The waiter then shares customers evenly across all the stands matching that rule.

Here's the clever part: you tell the waiter to look **only** for the shared tag `app=web` — and **not** the `track` tag. Because both the old and new stands wear `app=web`, the waiter happily sends customers to *all four*. The old:new ratio (3:1) becomes the traffic ratio (~25% to the new recipe). One counter, automatic split, no extra config.

The Service type is **ClusterIP** — a stable inside-the-cluster address and name (`web`) that never changes even as stands open and close.

**Watch out for:**

- **Do NOT put `track` in the Service selector.** If the clipboard says `app=web AND track=stable`, the waiter only sees the old stands and the canary gets **zero** customers — this is the #1 canary bug (and exactly what step 5 fixes).
- **The selector matches pod labels, not Deployment names.** The Service doesn't know "web-stable" exists; it only matches tags on pods.
- **`port` vs `targetPort`:** `port` (80) is the counter's number customers dial; `targetPort` (80) is the door on the stand. Here they're both 80, but they can differ.
- **No matching pods = no endpoints = connection refused**, even though the Service exists.
questions.deepDive:
## One Service fronting both — full rundown

### Mental model
A **Service** is a stable virtual IP + DNS name that load-balances across the **ready pods** matching its `selector`. For a label-based canary, the Service selects on the **shared** label only (`app=web`) so it fronts *both* Deployments; the replica ratio then becomes the traffic ratio.

> The golden rule: **put the shared label in the Service selector, never the distinguishing `track` label.**

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: canary-learn
spec:
  selector:
    app: web            # shared label ONLY — no track
  ports:
  - port: 80            # the Service's own port
    targetPort: 80      # the container port it forwards to
  # type: ClusterIP     # default
```

### port vs targetPort vs nodePort
| Field | Whose port | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `port` | the Service's cluster IP | required |
| `targetPort` | the container (pod) | defaults to `port` |
| `nodePort` | each node (NodePort/LoadBalancer only) | auto 30000–32767 |

### How selection + endpoints work
The EndpointSlice/Endpoints controller watches for pods that (a) match the selector and (b) are **Ready**, and lists their IPs:
```bash
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints web -o wide
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
```
With selector `app=web` and 3 stable + 1 canary ready pods, you should see **4** endpoint IPs.

### Service types (quick context)
| Type | Reachable from | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `ClusterIP` (default) | inside cluster | internal apps, this lab |
| `NodePort` | `<nodeIP>:<nodePort>` | basic external access |
| `LoadBalancer` | cloud LB | production external |
| `ExternalName` | CNAME alias | map to external DNS |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`track` in the selector breaks the canary.** `selector: {app: web, track: stable}` fronts only stable → canary gets 0 traffic. This is the single most common mistake (and step 5's whole scenario).
- **Selector matches pod labels, not Deployment/ReplicaSet names.** There is no "belongs to web-stable" concept at the Service layer.
- **Only Ready pods become endpoints.** No readiness → no traffic, even though the pod is Running.
- **Service selectors are plain `key: value` equality maps** (ANDed) — they do *not* support `matchExpressions` like Deployment selectors.
- **Empty endpoints** (`<none>`) usually means a selector/label mismatch or no ready pods — check with `get endpoints`.
- **`kubectl expose deploy web-stable`** would copy that Deployment's pod labels (`app=web, track=stable`) into the selector — wrong for canary. Write the Service by hand with just `app=web`.

### Quick reference
```bash
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web, namespace: canary-learn }
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
YAML

kubectl -n canary-learn get svc web
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints web -o wide   # expect 4 IPs
kubectl -n canary-learn get svc web -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'; echo
```

questions.title: Verify the traffic split
questions.teach:
The split is just the **endpoint ratio**: 3 stable + 1 canary ready pods = 4 endpoints, ~25% to the canary. Scale either Deployment to shift the split; scale canary up (and stable down) to **promote**, or delete the canary to roll back.

**Gotcha:** only **ready** pods become endpoints — a failing canary silently gets 0% traffic.
questions.prompt:
Confirm the canary is live: the `web` Service's endpoints must include pods from **both** Deployments — at least 3 from `web-stable` and at least 1 from `web-canary`.

Target: `web`'s endpoints include ≥3 web-stable pods AND ≥1 web-canary pod.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints web -o wide` — you should see 4 addresses. Make sure both Deployments' pods are Ready.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints web -o wide
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l app=web -L track

verification.description: web endpoints span both tracks (>=3 stable, >=1 canary)

questions.eli5:
Time to check your work: are customers actually reaching *both* the old and new stands? You peek at the waiter's **address list** — the list of stands the front counter is currently sending people to. In Kubernetes this list is called the **Endpoints**.

If everything's wired right, the list has **4 addresses**: 3 from the old stable stands and 1 from the new canary stand. That's your proof the split is live — roughly 25% of customers hit the new recipe, just because 1 of 4 stands runs it.

The key idea: the traffic split isn't magic or a percentage you typed anywhere. It's **just the count of addresses on the list**. Want more canary traffic? Open more canary stands (scale up). Want to roll back? Close the canary — its address drops off the list and 100% goes back to stable.

But a stand only gets onto the address list if it's **Ready** — meaning it has actually started and is prepared to serve. A stand that's still warming up, or crashing, isn't on the list.

**Watch out for:**

- **Only Ready pods become endpoints.** A canary that crash-loops or fails its readiness probe **silently** gets 0% traffic — the Service won't warn you, the address just never appears.
- **Count the addresses, don't assume.** Run `kubectl get endpoints web -o wide` and confirm you actually see 4, spanning both tracks.
- **A Pending or not-yet-Ready pod is invisible to the Service** even though `kubectl get pods` lists it.
- The split is **approximate** — kube-proxy spreads load roughly evenly, not exactly per request.
questions.deepDive:
## Verify the traffic split — full rundown

### Mental model
The traffic split is **not a configured percentage** — it's the live **endpoint ratio**. The Service forwards to its ready endpoints roughly evenly, so `canary endpoints / total endpoints` is the canary's traffic share. Verifying the canary is live means confirming the Service's Endpoints include pods from **both** tracks.

### Inspecting endpoints
```bash
# the address list the Service load-balances over
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints web -o wide

# modern equivalent (what controllers actually use)
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web -o wide

# map endpoint IPs back to pods + their track
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l app=web -o wide -L track
```
Expected: **4 addresses** — 3 on `track=stable` pods, 1 on `track=canary`.

### Why a pod might be missing from endpoints
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Pod `Pending` | not scheduled (resources/affinity) | check `describe pod` events |
| Pod `Running` but 0/1 Ready | readiness probe failing | fix probe / app health |
| Pod `CrashLoopBackOff` | container exits | `kubectl logs` |
| Pod not in endpoints, is Ready | label/selector mismatch | compare pod labels vs svc selector |

### Shifting & finishing the canary
```bash
# promote canary to carry everything
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-canary --replicas=4
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-stable --replicas=0

# roll back
kubectl -n canary-learn scale deploy web-canary --replicas=0
```

### Readiness gate detail
A pod becomes an endpoint only when **all** its containers pass their readiness probes (or have none). `publishNotReadyAddresses: true` on the Service overrides this, but default behaviour excludes not-ready pods — which is exactly why a broken canary quietly receives no traffic instead of serving errors.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Ready ≠ Running.** `kubectl get pods` showing `Running` isn't enough; check the `READY` column (`1/1`). Only Ready pods are endpoints.
- **Silent canary failure:** a crash-looping canary = 0 endpoints = 0% traffic, with no error from the Service.
- **`get endpoints` vs `describe svc`:** `describe svc web` also lists the `Endpoints:` line — handy one-shot check.
- **The split is probabilistic,** not a hard 25/75 per request; kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS) distributes connections.
- Confirm you're in the right **namespace** — empty output is often just a missing `-n canary-learn`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints web -o wide           # expect 4 IPs
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l app=web -L track         # 3 stable + 1 canary, all 1/1 Ready
kubectl -n canary-learn describe svc web | grep -i endpoints
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: canary gets no traffic
questions.teach:
A canary getting **no** traffic usually means the Service selector is **too specific** — it includes `track=stable`, so canary pods aren't selected. Loosen it to the shared label only.

**Gotcha:** patching `selector:{app:pay}` *merges* — `track` stays; you must set `track: null` (or `kubectl edit`) to actually remove the key.
questions.prompt:
Service `pay` in `canary-learn` fronts only its stable pods — `pay-canary` gets no traffic. Diagnose why and fix it so **both** are served. Don't delete it.

Target: `pay`'s endpoints include `pay-canary` pods.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n canary-learn get svc pay -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'` → it has `track: stable`. Remove that: `kubectl -n canary-learn patch svc pay -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"pay","track":null}}}'` (or edit to `selector: {app: pay}`).
questions.solution:
# patching selector:{app:pay} MERGES — track:stable would remain; set track:null to remove it
kubectl -n canary-learn patch svc pay -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"pay","track":null}}}'
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints pay -o wide

verification.description: pay endpoints now include pay-canary pods (selector loosened)

questions.eli5:
Here's a broken shop to fix. There's a second front counter called `pay`, and its new canary stand is getting **zero** customers — all traffic goes to the old stands. Your job: figure out why, and fix it without tearing the counter down.

The culprit is almost always the waiter's clipboard (the Service **selector**) being **too picky**. Instead of just "send to anything tagged `app=pay`," the clipboard says "send only to things tagged `app=pay` **AND** `track=stable`." Since the canary stands wear `track=canary`, the waiter literally never sees them. Fix: remove the `track=stable` line so the clipboard only checks `app=pay` again.

Now the sneaky part. When you "patch" (edit) the selector in Kubernetes, it **merges** your change into what's already there — like adding sticky notes rather than replacing the whole clipboard. So if you patch `selector: {app: pay}`, the old `track: stable` line **stays**, and nothing improves! To actually *delete* that line, you have to explicitly say "erase it" by setting `track: null`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Strategic-merge patch doesn't remove keys** — you must set the unwanted key to **`null`** to delete it. Patching just `{app: pay}` leaves `track: stable` in place.
- **Diagnose first:** read the live selector with `kubectl get svc pay -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'` before changing anything.
- **Don't delete the Service** — the task says fix it in place (`kubectl edit svc pay` or a patch both work).
- After fixing, **verify the endpoints** actually now include the canary pods — don't assume.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix: canary gets no traffic — full rundown

### Mental model
A canary getting **zero** traffic almost always means the Service selector is **too specific** — it includes the distinguishing label (`track=stable`), so canary pods never match. The fix is to **loosen** the selector to the shared label only. The twist: a strategic-merge patch *adds/overwrites* keys but does **not remove** them — you must set the unwanted key to `null`.

### Diagnose
```bash
# 1. Is the canary pod actually missing from endpoints?
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints pay -o wide
kubectl -n canary-learn get pods -l app=pay -L track -o wide

# 2. What does the Service actually select?
kubectl -n canary-learn get svc pay -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'; echo
# -> {"app":"pay","track":"stable"}   <-- the bug
```
The canary pods carry `track=canary`, so `track=stable` in the selector excludes them.

### Fix — and the merge gotcha
```bash
# WRONG: merge keeps the existing track key
kubectl -n canary-learn patch svc pay -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"pay"}}}'
# resulting selector: {"app":"pay","track":"stable"}  <-- unchanged bug!

# RIGHT: explicitly delete the key with null
kubectl -n canary-learn patch svc pay \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"pay","track":null}}}'
# resulting selector: {"app":"pay"}

# verify
kubectl -n canary-learn get svc pay -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'; echo
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints pay -o wide    # now includes canary IPs
```

### Patch strategies compared
| Method | Default `--type` | Removes a key? |
|---|---|---|
| `kubectl patch -p '{...}'` | strategic merge | only via explicit `null` |
| `kubectl patch --type=merge -p '{...}'` | JSON merge (RFC 7386) | only via explicit `null` |
| `kubectl patch --type=json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/selector/track"}]'` | JSON patch | yes, `remove` op |
| `kubectl edit svc pay` | interactive | yes — just delete the line |

For a plain Service selector, either `track: null` or `kubectl edit` (delete the `track:` line) works; `--type=json` with a `remove` op is the most explicit.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Merge patches never drop keys.** Setting `selector:{app:pay}` leaves `track:stable` untouched. Use `null`, a JSON-patch `remove`, or `edit`.
- **Diagnose before you patch** — read `.spec.selector` so you fix the real cause, not a guess.
- **Don't delete and recreate** when the task says fix in place; and recreating would change the ClusterIP, breaking existing DNS consumers.
- **After patching, re-check endpoints** — a correct selector still needs the canary pods to be **Ready** to appear.
- Watch the **quoting**: `null` is a JSON literal (no quotes); `"null"` would set the string "null" as a label value.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n canary-learn get svc pay -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'; echo   # diagnose
kubectl -n canary-learn patch svc pay \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"pay","track":null}}}'                    # fix
kubectl -n canary-learn get endpoints pay -o wide                          # verify
```
